concepts.title: Character Capacity of ASCII and ISCII Codes

questions.q: Using the method 'Character Capacity of ASCII and ISCII Codes', work with: code_bits = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of ascii_share.
Take the relation taught for 'Character Capacity of ASCII and ISCII Codes' and work with: code_bits = 8. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of ascii_share.
Explain in your own words what 'Character Capacity of ASCII and ISCII Codes' refers to.
questions.a: Keyboard characters reach a computer as numeric codes: ASCII assigns 7-bit values covering 128 English characters, while the 8-bit ISCII scheme keeps those 128 codes and adds another 128 slots for Indian script symbols.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Character Capacity of ASCII and ISCII Codes'.
questions.a: A code of n bits can label exactly 2 raised to n different characters.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Character Capacity of ASCII and ISCII Codes', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Positional Value in a Number System

questions.q: Using the method 'Positional Value in a Number System', work with: base = 40, position = 4, symbol = 512. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of digit_share.
Take the relation taught for 'Positional Value in a Number System' and work with: base = 60, position = 3, symbol = 512. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of digit_share.
Explain in your own words what 'Positional Value in a Number System' refers to.
questions.a: Every number system has a base equal to its count of distinct symbols, and each symbol's worth depends on its slot: the positional worth is the base raised to the slot number, counted from zero at the right of the integer part.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Positional Value in a Number System'.
questions.a: Slot zero sits at the right of the integer part, and each step left raises the power of the base by one.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Positional Value in a Number System', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Binary to Decimal Conversion', work with: d0 = 80, d1 = 4, d2 = 300, d3 = 15. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of dec_val.
Take the relation taught for 'Binary to Decimal Conversion' and work with: d0 = 45, d1 = 150, d2 = 80, d3 = 400. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of dec_val.
Explain in your own words what 'Binary to Decimal Conversion' refers to.
questions.a: A binary string names a decimal value: weight each bit by the matching power of two, counting from 1 at the rightmost bit, and add all the weighted shares together.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Binary to Decimal Conversion'.
questions.a: Powers of two double from right to left, so each bit position is worth twice the one after it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Binary to Decimal Conversion', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Decimal to Binary by Repeated Division

questions.q: Using the method 'Decimal to Binary by Repeated Division', work with: dec = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of digits.
Take the relation taught for 'Decimal to Binary by Repeated Division' and work with: dec = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of digits.
Explain in your own words what 'Decimal to Binary by Repeated Division' refers to.
questions.a: To rewrite a decimal number in binary, divide it by 2 over and over, jot down each remainder, stop when the quotient reaches zero, and then read the remainders from last to first.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Decimal to Binary by Repeated Division'.
questions.a: Remainders appear least-significant bit first, which is why the collected column is read upside down.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Decimal to Binary by Repeated Division', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Binary Grouping into Octal and Hexadecimal

questions.q: Using the method 'Binary Grouping into Octal and Hexadecimal', work with: b0 = 24, b1 = 50, b2 = 12, b3 = 360, b4 = 500, b5 = 6. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of octal_digits.

Take the relation taught for 'Binary Grouping into Octal and Hexadecimal' and work with: b0 = 25, b1 = 10, b2 = 240, b3 = 6, b4 = 18, b5 = 3. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of octal_digits.
Explain in your own words what 'Binary Grouping into Octal and Hexadecimal' refers to.
questions.a: Because 8 and 16 are powers of two, a binary string converts to octal or hexadecimal by cutting it into chunks of 3 or 4 bits from the right and swapping each chunk for its single digit.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Binary Grouping into Octal and Hexadecimal'.
questions.a: Three bits make one octal digit and four bits make one hexadecimal symbol, so long bit strings shrink sharply.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Binary Grouping into Octal and Hexadecimal', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Hexadecimal Colour Codes for Web Pages

questions.q: Using the method 'Hexadecimal Colour Codes for Web Pages', work with: components = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of palette.
Take the relation taught for 'Hexadecimal Colour Codes for Web Pages' and work with: components = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of palette.
Explain in your own words what 'Hexadecimal Colour Codes for Web Pages' refers to.
questions.a: A screen colour mixes red, green and blue, each stored as one byte, so a colour needs 24 bits; writing each byte as a two-symbol hexadecimal pair gives compact codes such as FF0000 for pure red.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Hexadecimal Colour Codes for Web Pages'.
questions.a: One byte per channel means 24 bits per colour, which folds into six hexadecimal symbols.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Hexadecimal Colour Codes for Web Pages', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Fractional Binary to Decimal', work with: f1 = 4, f2 = 500, f3 = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of frac_val.
Take the relation taught for 'Fractional Binary to Decimal' and work with: f1 = 3, f2 = 240, f3 = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of frac_val.
Explain in your own words what 'Fractional Binary to Decimal' refers to.
questions.a: Bits after the binary point carry negative powers of two: the first is one half, the next one quarter, then one eighth, and the decimal value is the sum of these fractional shares.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fractional Binary to Decimal'.
questions.a: Left of the point the powers of two grow; right of it they halve from one half downwards.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Fractional Binary to Decimal', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Unicode and UTF Encodings' refers to.
questions.a: Unicode assigns one number to every character of every written language, so text survives across devices and programs; its UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 forms differ in how many bits each character occupies.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Unicode and UTF Encodings'.
questions.a: Codes 0 to 128 agree with ASCII, which keeps ordinary English text unchanged under Unicode.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Unicode and UTF Encodings', in plain ASCII form.
